statement: In 24 healthy, screened adults (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30; at most 20 lifetime uses of psychedelics or MDMA) who each took MDMA (100 mg) and LSD (100 µg) at the same time, compared with each drug alone and with a dummy, one per hospital session at least 10 days apart, in block-randomized, counterbalanced order under double-blind, double-dummy conditions in a calm hospital room (study conditions), the combination raised blood pressure and heart rate more than LSD alone, to about the levels of MDMA alone, but not body temperature, did not significantly lower the unwanted effects people rated on LSD, raised LSD's blood levels, and lowered and delayed MDMA's peak (Straumann et al., 2023). Heart and blood pressure (average of each person's highest value, ± SEM): systolic 150 ± 2.9 mmHg with both drugs against 137 ± 2.7 with LSD alone (p < 0.001), 148 ± 2.9 with MDMA alone (not significantly different) and 124 ± 2.4 with the dummy; diastolic 90 against 85 (p < 0.05), 89 and 77; heart rate 100 ± 3.6 beats a minute against 92 ± 4.5 (p < 0.05), 95 and 77. Temperature: 37.5 ± 0.08 °C with both drugs against 37.4 ± 0.06 with LSD alone (not significantly different), 37.3 with MDMA alone (lower than with both drugs, p < 0.05) and 37.0 with the dummy. Unwanted effects: complaint scores in the first 12 hours were 15 (± 2.2) with both drugs and 15 (± 1.9) with LSD alone (8.6 with MDMA alone, 1.9 with the dummy), and from 12 to 24 hours 5.5 against 3.1 (not significantly different); ratings of a bad drug effect (14 against 18 out of 100) and of fear (8.2 against 13) did not differ significantly from LSD alone; headache, lack of energy, loss of appetite and dry mouth were reported about as often with either drug or both; no severe adverse event occurred. On nausea the paper contradicts itself: its results say nausea on the complaint list was more frequent with MDMA than with LSD, its table shows nausea ratings lower with MDMA (7.9 out of 100) than with LSD (25) or both drugs (21), and its discussion says nausea was about as frequent with both drugs as with either alone; the item counts are in a supplement that was not read. Late in the LSD response the authors note trend-level, non-significant signs of lower well-being and more depressed mood with both drugs in some people. Blood levels: with MDMA, LSD's peak was 2.1 against 1.9 ng/mL (p < 0.05), its half-life 5.2 against 3.9 hours (p < 0.001) and its total exposure 19 against 14 ng·h/mL (p < 0.01; about a third more, editors' calculation); with LSD, MDMA's peak was 208 against 233 ng/mL (p < 0.001; about a tenth lower, editors' calculation) and came later, at 3.5 against 2.8 hours (p < 0.01), with total exposure unchanged; the paper's text and abstract mention only the change in LSD's levels. The authors attribute the higher LSD levels to MDMA blocking a liver enzyme (CYP2D6), which they inferred from other studies and did not measure. Their statement that they found no sign of greater serotonin toxicity rests on 24 healthy people given one pair of doses together in a calm room, which cannot show rare or setting-dependent harms; other doses, other timing, repeated doses, heat, dancing, alcohol or other drugs, and people with heart or psychiatric conditions or on interacting medicines were not studied. Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: What if you take LSD and MDMA at the same time? In one lab study, 24 healthy adults each had four hospital days: LSD, MDMA, both at once, or a dummy, in random order and without being told which. With both, blood pressure and heart rate went higher than on LSD alone: top blood pressure averaged 150, against 137 on LSD alone and 148 on MDMA alone, and heart rate 100 beats a minute, against 92 and 95. Body temperature was no higher than on LSD alone. Bad feelings, fear and the number of complaints were not clearly lower than on LSD alone, and on nausea the paper contradicts itself. The two drugs changed each other's blood levels: more LSD stayed in the blood for longer, while MDMA peaked lower and later. Nobody had a serious problem, but this was one amount of each drug, taken together by healthy people in a calm hospital room, so it says little about rare dangers or about a party.
population: 24 healthy, screened adults (12 women, 12 men; mean age 30, range 25 to 54), recruited by word of mouth or from a pool of people interested in psychedelic trials, and paid; 12 had used a psychedelic and 9 MDMA before (1 to 13 times); excluded were more than 20 lifetime uses of hallucinogens or MDMA, illicit drug use in the past 2 months (cannabis excepted), a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder and interfering medicines; Basel
exposure: MDMA 100 mg (four 25 mg capsules; analysed 25.40 mg each) and LSD base 100 µg (oral solution; analysed content 92.5 µg) taken at the same time, double-blind and double-dummy, in a calm hospital room with one investigator (study conditions)
comparator: LSD 100 µg alone, MDMA 100 mg alone and placebo in the same people, at least 10 days apart, in block-randomized, counterbalanced order
outcome: Peak blood pressure, heart rate, body temperature and pupil size; complaint scores for 0 to 12 and 12 to 24 hours, self-rated bad drug effect, fear and nausea, and adverse events; blood levels of LSD and MDMA over 24 hours
magnitude: Straumann et al. (2023), 24 people (Table 1, mean ± SEM; placebo, MDMA, LSD, LSD + MDMA; F(3,69); Tukey tests): systolic 124 ± 2.4, 148 ± 2.9, 137 ± 2.7 and 150 ± 2.9 mmHg (combination against LSD p < 0.001, against MDMA not significant); diastolic 77 ± 1.7, 89 ± 1.4, 85 ± 1.8 and 90 ± 1.4 (combination against LSD p < 0.05); mean arterial 92, 107, 102 and 109 (combination against LSD p < 0.001); heart rate 77 ± 2.6, 95 ± 3.4, 92 ± 4.5 and 100 ± 3.6 bpm (combination against LSD p < 0.05, against MDMA not significant); rate-pressure product 9290, 13698, 12385 and 14678 mmHg × bpm (combination against LSD p < 0.001); body temperature 37.0 ± 0.05, 37.3 ± 0.07, 37.4 ± 0.06 and 37.5 ± 0.08 °C (combination against LSD not significant, against MDMA p < 0.05; MDMA against LSD not significant); pupil size 6.0, 7.1, 7.0 and 7.2 mm (combination against LSD p < 0.05; n = 23). Complaints: acute (0–12 h) 1.9 ± 1.1, 8.6 ± 1.8, 15 ± 1.9 and 15 ± 2.2 (combination against LSD not significant); subacute (12–24 h) −0.2 ± 0.5, 2.5 ± 0.9, 3.1 ± 1.0 and 5.5 ± 1.4 (combination against LSD not significant, against MDMA p < 0.05). Visual analogue peaks (% of maximum): bad drug effect 0.2, 6.4, 18 and 14 (combination against LSD not significant); fear 0.2, 2.3, 13 and 8.2 (not significant); nausea 1.0, 7.9, 25 and 21 (MDMA lower than LSD, p < 0.001, and than the combination, p < 0.05; LSD against combination not significant). Blood levels (Table 2, geometric mean, 95% CI; paired t-tests): LSD peak 1.9 (1.7–2.1) alone and 2.1 (1.9–2.3) ng/mL with MDMA (p < 0.05); half-life 3.9 (3.5–4.4) and 5.2 (4.6–5.9) h (p < 0.001); AUC∞ 14 (12–17) and 19 (16–22) ng·h/mL (p < 0.01); apparent clearance 6.9 and 5.3 L/h (p < 0.01); time to peak 1.6 h in both. MDMA peak 233 (215–252) alone and 208 (189–228) ng/mL with LSD (p < 0.001); time to peak 2.8 (2.5–3.2) and 3.5 (3.0–4.0) h (p < 0.01); half-life 8.3 and 8.2 h; AUC∞ 3083 and 3068 ng·h/mL (some MDMA-alone values from 23 people). Editors' calculation from the printed means: LSD AUC∞ about 36% higher, MDMA peak about 11% lower. No severe adverse events.

evidence.extracted: Double-blind, placebo-controlled, double-dummy crossover, registered (NCT04516902), block-randomized with counterbalanced order, at least 10 days between sessions: placebo, MDMA 100 mg, LSD 100 µg, and LSD 100 µg with MDMA 100 mg at the same time, given at 9:00 after a standardized breakfast in a calm hospital room with one investigator; 13-h sessions with a 24-h follow-up. 24 healthy participants (12 men, 12 women; age 30 ± 7, range 25–54), recruited by word of mouth or from volunteers interested in a psychedelic trial, paid; 12 had used a psychedelic, 9 MDMA (1–13 times), 4 no illicit drug other than cannabis. Exclusions included more than 20 lifetime uses of hallucinogens or MDMA, illicit drug use in the past 2 months (cannabis excepted) and a personal or first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder. LSD base solution, analysed 92.5 ± 1.89 µg per 100 µg unit; MDMA hydrochloride capsules, analysed 25.40 ± 0.48 mg per 25 mg capsule.

risk_of_bias.note: Registered, block-randomized, counterbalanced, double-dummy crossover with complete data (card sc_straumann_2023: RoB 2 some concerns). Blood pressure, heart rate, temperature and drug levels are objective; the unwanted-effect scores and ratings are self-reports under imperfect blinding, allocation concealment is not described, most item-level statistics are in an unread supplement, the paper's three statements on nausea disagree, and the text leaves out LSD's effect on MDMA's levels.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: one pair of doses taken together, healthy screened volunteers with limited drug experience, a calm hospital room, which the statement says; it claims nothing about party settings, other doses or timing, or rare harms.

imprecision.note: 24 people. The rises in blood pressure and heart rate against LSD alone are significant, but the findings that temperature and unwanted effects were no higher, or no lower, than with LSD alone are non-significant comparisons, not shown equivalence, and rare harms such as serotonin toxicity cannot be detected in 24 people.

grade.reasoning: Randomized within-person crossover: starts high (METHODS 6.3). Risk of bias −1 and imprecision −1 give low. The larger blood-pressure and heart-rate rises with both drugs than with LSD alone, objective and significant in the same people, would be rated moderate on their own; the findings on temperature and unwanted effects rest on non-significant tests and are worded as such. Status single study: the first controlled human study of the combination, from one laboratory. The claim leaves out how strong or long the good effects felt, and gives no timing.

verification.flag_note: Question 10 of round pdf-2026-11-14 (theme 23). Left out under the brief: comparisons of how strong or long the good effects felt, including the 1.5 h longer 'any drug effect' duration with both drugs (Results › Subjective drug effects, 3rd paragraph, p. 1842); the editor may decide whether the longer duration belongs here as a risk fact. Also left out: the authors' untested suggestion (Discussion, 4th paragraph, p. 1845) that antidepressants that block CYP2D6 could raise LSD levels similarly, a possible separate question on LSD with medicines. Not read: the online supplement (doi:10.1038/s41386-023-01609-0), whose Table S6 would settle the nausea contradiction; the registry record NCT04516902.
